title: Molecular Spectroscopy & NMR
subject: Chemical Physics
summary: The physics behind the spectra an organic chemist reads every day. Light–matter interaction (the dipole Hamiltonian, Fermi's golden rule, Einstein coefficients, symmetry selection rules, line shapes), rotational and vibrational spectroscopy (rotor and populations, normal modes from the Hessian, anharmonicity, IR versus Raman), and electronic spectroscopy (Born–Oppenheimer, Franck–Condon, Jablonski diagrams as rate physics) lead into the core of the course: magnetic resonance as spin dynamics. That covers the Zeeman Hamiltonian, the rotating frame, RF pulses as rotations, Bloch equations, the FID as a Fourier transform, shielding and J-coupling (weak and strong), the density operator and product operators, INEPT, 2D NMR as a two-time Fourier transform, and relaxation theory (spectral densities, BPP, NOE) grounded in statistical mechanics, with short closing lessons on MRI and EPR.

units.title: Light–Matter Interaction and Line Shapes
units.summary: How a molecule absorbs and emits: the dipole interaction, Fermi's golden rule, Einstein coefficients, symmetry selection rules, and why lines have a width (the Lorentzian is the Fourier transform of exponential decay, the same fact that gives the NMR linewidth).

lessons.title: Spectroscopy as Energy-Level Reading: Scales and Populations
objectives: Convert between frequency, wavenumber, wavelength and molar energy (Hz, cm⁻¹, nm, kJ/mol) and place NMR, microwave rotation, IR vibration and UV–vis electronic transitions on one energy axis.

Compute the thermal population difference of a two-level transition from the Boltzmann factor, and explain why it sets sensitivity: NMR polarization is about 10⁻⁵ at room temperature while IR and UV transitions start almost entirely from the ground state.

Explain what the vertical axis of a spectrum measures (absorption rate versus frequency) and which question each regime answers about a molecule (rotation, bond stiffness, electronic structure, spin environment).

lectures.title: Lecture 19: Spectroscopy: Probing Molecules with Light

demoIdeas: Log-frequency ruler from radio to UV: pick a transition type and a temperature, see ΔE/kT, the Boltzmann population bars and the net polarization; slide B0 from 1 T to 23 T and watch the NMR polarization (and the ¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁵N differences) change.

lessons.title: The Semiclassical Dipole Hamiltonian and Rabi Oscillations
objectives: Write the semiclassical interaction H′(t) = −μ̂·E(t) for a molecule in a classical light field, state the electric-dipole approximation and when it fails (wavelength ≫ molecular size), and name the magnetic-dipole analogue −μ̂·B that drives NMR.
Solve the driven two-level problem in the rotating-wave approximation: give the Rabi frequency Ω = μ₁₂E₀/ħ and the detuned Rabi formula, and explain why population oscillates between the levels.
Explain why a strong coherent field produces oscillations (the NMR pulse regime) while a weak broadband field gives a steady rate (the next lesson).

lectures.title: Interaction of Light and Matter (lecture 4 notes)
Lecture 31: Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory II. H is Time-Dependent: Two-Level Problem

demoIdeas: Rabi oscillation explorer: sliders for field amplitude and detuning; plot P₂(t) and the Bloch-vector path; overlay the weak-field perturbative result and show where it breaks down.

lessons.title: Fermi's Golden Rule and What an Absorption Intensity Measures
objectives: State Fermi's golden rule w = (2π/ħ)|V_fi|²ρ(E_f) and derive it from first-order time-dependent perturbation theory, showing how the sin²(ωt/2)/ω² kernel becomes a δ-function so that probability grows linearly in time.

Apply it to absorption: the rate is proportional to |μ_fi|² times the light intensity times a line-shape function, so the integrated band area measures |μ_fi|² while the band shape encodes the final-state distribution.
Explain when the golden rule fails (strong, short or coherent excitation, discrete isolated levels) and connect the failure to the Rabi regime and to NMR pulses.

lectures.title: Lecture 30: Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory I. H is Time-Independent, Zewail Wavepacket

demoIdeas: Golden-rule kernel: watch P(ω,t) as t grows. The peak height grows as t², the width shrinks as 1/t and the area grows as t, which is why the rate becomes constant. Slider for a final-state continuum width to see when the linear regime holds.

lessons.title: Einstein Coefficients, Transition Dipoles and Radiative Lifetimes
objectives: Derive A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³ and B₁₂ = B₂₁ (equal degeneracies) by demanding that the rate equations reproduce Planck's blackbody law, and write A₂₁ in terms of the transition dipole.

Compute a radiative lifetime from |μ₁₂| and ν, and compare a visible electronic transition (nanoseconds) with a 600 MHz nuclear-spin transition (astronomically long), concluding that NMR relaxation cannot be spontaneous emission.
Use the ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission, 1/(e^{hν/kT} − 1), to explain why microwave/RF transitions are dominated by stimulated processes and why lasers need population inversion.
demoIdeas: Thermal-radiation two-level system: sliders for temperature and transition frequency; plot the stimulated-to-spontaneous ratio 1/(e^{hν/kT}−1) and the equilibrium populations, marking the crossover at hν ≈ kT.

lessons.title: Transition Dipoles and Selection Rules from Symmetry
objectives: Explain a selection rule as the vanishing of ⟨f|μ̂|i⟩ by symmetry: the integral is nonzero only if Γ_f ⊗ Γ_(x,y,z) ⊗ Γ_i contains the totally symmetric representation.
Apply the rule to parity (Laporte), spin (ΔS = 0, since μ̂ does not act on spin) and a worked C₂ᵥ example, and state the polarization each allowed transition has.
Distinguish forbidden from weak: say how vibronic coupling, spin–orbit coupling and magnetic-dipole or quadrupole terms let a weak band appear (the n→π* carbonyl band near 300 nm, ε ≈ 20–100).

demoIdeas: Symmetry-product calculator: choose a point group (C₂ᵥ, D₂ₕ, C₃ᵥ), an initial and final state, and see the direct-product table, whether the A₁ component appears, and which polarization (x, y, z) is allowed.

lessons.title: Line Shapes: Natural, Doppler and Pressure Broadening
objectives: Show that a damped oscillation e^{iω₀t − t/T₂} has a Lorentzian Fourier transform with FWHM 1/(πT₂) in Hz, and relate natural linewidth to excited-state lifetime, Δν = 1/(2πτ).

Distinguish homogeneous (Lorentzian: natural, collisional, T₂) from inhomogeneous (Gaussian: Doppler, field inhomogeneity) broadening, compute the Doppler width ν₀√(8kT ln2/mc²), and describe the Voigt profile as their convolution.
Compare the widths a chemist sees: gas-phase IR lines (~100 MHz Doppler), fluorescence (~30 MHz lifetime width) and solution NMR lines (≈ 1 Hz), and say which mechanism sets each.

demoIdeas: Line-shape lab: side-by-side time-domain decay and its Fourier transform; sliders for T₂ (Lorentzian), Doppler width (Gaussian) and their Voigt convolution, with a live readout of FWHM, area and peak height.

units.title: Rotational and Vibrational Spectroscopy
units.summary: Microwave and infrared spectra as direct readouts of moments of inertia and force constants: rotors and populations, normal modes from the Hessian (the same Hessian a DFT job returns), anharmonicity, IR versus Raman selection by symmetry, and overtones.

lessons.title: The Rigid Rotor and Microwave Spectra
objectives: Write E_J = hcB·J(J+1) with B = ħ/(4πcI) and I = μr², and derive the line positions ν = 2B(J+1) for J → J+1 from the selection rule ΔJ = ±1.
Extract a bond length from a measured line (e.g. CO at 115.27 GHz) and explain why isotopic substitution shifts the lines.
Explain why a microwave absorption spectrum needs a permanent dipole (so H₂, N₂, CO₂ and CH₄ are silent) and what the rotational Raman rule ΔJ = ±2 adds.

lectures.title: Lecture 17: Rigid Rotor I. Orbital Angular Momentum

lectures.source: MIT OCW 5.80 Small-Molecule Spectroscopy and Dynamics (Fall 2008)
lectures.title: Lecture 22: Rotation of polyatomic molecules I

demoIdeas: Rotor ladder with transition arrows: choose masses and bond length, see the J levels, the equally spaced microwave lines at 2B(J+1), and the isotopologue shift when ¹²C is replaced by ¹³C.

lessons.title: Rotational Populations, Intensities and Nuclear-Spin Statistics
objectives: Compute rotational populations N_J ∝ (2J+1)exp(−hcBJ(J+1)/kT), find the most populated level J_max ≈ √(kT/2hcB) − ½, and explain the (2J+1) degeneracy as the origin of an intensity maximum away from J = 0.
Predict how a rotational spectrum changes with temperature and use the intensity envelope as a thermometer.
Explain ortho/para hydrogen: why nuclear-spin symmetry forces alternate J levels and a 3:1 intensity alternation, and how para-hydrogen is used as a hyperpolarization source for NMR.
demoIdeas: Rotational stick spectrum with sliders for temperature and B; shows the shifting intensity envelope and J_max. A toggle switches on H₂ nuclear-spin statistics (3:1 alternation) and the ortho/para equilibrium ratio versus temperature.

lessons.title: Centrifugal Distortion and Symmetric Tops
objectives: Derive centrifugal distortion by treating the bond as a spring, E_J = BJ(J+1) − DJ²(J+1)² with D = 4B³/ω̃ₑ², and estimate how far lines shift from the rigid-rotor pattern at high J.
Classify rotors as linear, spherical, symmetric or asymmetric tops from the three moments of inertia, and write the symmetric-top levels E(J,K) = BJ(J+1) + (A − B)K² with the rules ΔJ = ±1, ΔK = 0.
Explain how rotational constants from several isotopologues give a molecular structure (the basis of microwave structure determination).

lectures.title: Lecture 24: Pure rotation spectra of polyatomic molecules

demoIdeas: Non-rigid rotor: slider for D (set by the force constant) compresses the line spacing as J grows; a second panel shows the symmetric-top K-ladder and the effect of A and B on a prolate versus an oblate top.

lessons.title: Normal Modes from the Mass-Weighted Hessian
objectives: Expand the potential to second order about a minimum, build the mass-weighted Hessian F_ij/√(m_i m_j), and show that its eigenvalues are ω² and its eigenvectors are decoupled normal coordinates, giving 3N − 6 (linear: 3N − 5) vibrations.
Compute by hand the stretching modes of a symmetric linear triatomic (the CO₂ toy model) and interpret the symmetric and antisymmetric eigenvectors.
Connect the calculation to a DFT frequency job (the Hessian from quantum chemistry) and to isotope shifts, where ω ∝ 1/√m so H → D lowers an X–H stretch by about 1/√2.

lessons.title: Anharmonicity and the Morse Oscillator
objectives: Write the Morse potential and its levels E_v = ħω(v+½) − ħωx_e(v+½)² with x_e = ħω/4D_e, and explain why level spacing shrinks toward dissociation.
Predict the positions of the fundamental (ω − 2ωx_e) and first overtone (2ω − 6ωx_e) and extract ω_e, ω_ex_e and a dissociation-energy estimate from them (Birge–Sponer).
Explain why anharmonicity makes Δv = ±2, ±3 weakly allowed, and separate mechanical anharmonicity (potential shape) from electrical anharmonicity (non-linear dipole function).

demoIdeas: Morse versus harmonic well: sliders for D_e and a; show the levels, the shrinking spacings, the fundamental and overtone positions, and a Birge–Sponer plot extrapolated to the dissociation limit.

lessons.title: IR versus Raman Activity from Symmetry
objectives: Derive IR activity (dμ/dQ ≠ 0) and Raman activity (dα/dQ ≠ 0) from the Taylor expansion of dipole and polarizability in the normal coordinate, and state the symmetry criterion (modes transforming like x, y, z for IR; like xx, xy, … for Raman).
Apply the criteria with a character table to CO₂ (rule of mutual exclusion in a centrosymmetric molecule) and H₂O (all three modes active).

Explain Raman scattering as inelastic two-photon scattering, compute the anti-Stokes/Stokes intensity ratio, and say which functional groups the organic chemist sees in one technique but not the other (symmetric C≡C).

demoIdeas: Mode inspector: choose CO₂, H₂O or C₂H₂, animate each normal mode with arrows for the dipole change and an ellipsoid for the polarizability change, and see the resulting IR/Raman label with the symmetry label.

lessons.title: Rotation–Vibration Spectra: P and R Branches
objectives: Combine E(v,J) = ω(v+½) + B_vJ(J+1) to derive the P- and R-branch positions, including the (B₁ − B₀)J² term, and explain the band-origin gap and the absent Q branch for a closed-shell diatomic.
Extract B₀, B₁ and the bond-length change on excitation from combination differences, and explain why the R branch converges while the P branch spreads out.
Explain the HCl isotope doublets (³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl) and why liquid-phase IR shows only broad envelopes (rotation is quenched by collisions).
demoIdeas: Rovibrational band builder: sliders for B₀, B₁ and temperature give the P/R stick spectrum and intensity envelope; a toggle adds the ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl isotopologues and a collision-broadening slider collapses the gas-phase lines into the liquid-phase envelope.

lessons.title: Overtones, Combination Bands and Fermi Resonance
objectives: Predict overtone and combination-band positions from fundamentals and anharmonic constants, and explain the intensity drop (~10–100 times weaker per quantum).
Treat Fermi resonance as a two-level mixing problem: levels split by √(Δ² + 4W²), intensity is shared between the two bands, and the CO₂ 1388/1286 cm⁻¹ dyad and the aldehyde C–H doublet are examples.
Describe the local-mode picture of X–H overtones (C–H, O–H, N–H in the near-IR) and why NIR bands carry chemical information despite being weak.
demoIdeas: Fermi-resonance avoided crossing: slide the unperturbed gap through zero for a chosen coupling W and watch the two levels repel while the intensity bars exchange weight.

units.title: Electronic Spectroscopy
units.summary: Electronic transitions as vertical jumps between potential energy surfaces: Born–Oppenheimer, Franck–Condon factors and vibronic structure, then fluorescence and phosphorescence treated as competing first-order rate processes in a Jablonski diagram.

lessons.title: The Born–Oppenheimer Approximation and Potential Energy Surfaces
objectives: Show how the Born–Oppenheimer separation Ψ ≈ ψ_el(r;R)χ(R) arises from the mass ratio (expansion parameter κ = (m_e/M)^{1/4}), and define the potential energy surface as the electronic energy at fixed nuclear positions.
Identify what is neglected (nuclear kinetic-energy operator acting on ψ_el, i.e. non-adiabatic coupling) and when it matters (avoided crossings, conical intersections, light atoms).
Use the ordering of energy scales 1 : κ² : κ⁴ (electronic : vibrational : rotational) to explain why the three kinds of spectra appear in different spectral regions.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation

lectures.source: MIT OCW 5.80 Small-Molecule Spectroscopy and Dynamics (Fall 2008)
lectures.title: Lecture 9: The Born–Oppenheimer approach to transitions

demoIdeas: Avoided crossing of two surfaces: a coupling slider moves from diabatic crossing to adiabatic avoided crossing; a mass slider shows the non-adiabatic coupling peak and the probability of hopping between surfaces.

lessons.title: Franck–Condon Factors and Vertical Transitions
objectives: Derive the vibronic transition moment within the Born–Oppenheimer and Condon approximations, μ_fi ≈ μ_el⟨χ_v′|χ_v⟩, so that intensity is proportional to the Franck–Condon factor |⟨χ_v′|χ_v⟩|².
Compute Franck–Condon factors for two displaced oscillators of equal frequency: a Poisson distribution e^{−S}S^n/n! with Huang–Rhys factor S = mωΔ²/2ħ, whose most intense line is near n ≈ S.
Predict from the geometry change whether the 0–0 band or a long progression dominates (small versus large displacement), and state that the factors sum to one.

demoIdeas: Displaced oscillators: sliders for the displacement Δ and the frequency change; show the two wells, the overlap of ground-state wavefunction with each excited vibrational level, and the vibronic stick spectrum, with a Poisson overlay.

lessons.title: Vibronic Structure, Stokes Shift and Electronic Selection Rules
objectives: Read an absorption/emission pair: identify the 0–0 line, the mirror-image relation and the Stokes shift (≈ 2Sħω in the displaced-oscillator model), and explain why solution spectra of organic dyes are broad.

State the electronic selection rules (ΔS = 0, Laporte, orbital symmetry) and estimate an oscillator strength from a molar absorption spectrum, f ≈ 4.32 × 10⁻⁹ ∫ε dν̃; contrast n→π* (ε ~ 10²) with π→π* (ε ~ 10⁴).
Explain how vibronic (Herzberg–Teller) coupling lends intensity to symmetry-forbidden bands such as the benzene 260 nm system.

demoIdeas: Absorption/emission synthesizer: Franck–Condon progression convolved with homogeneous and solvent (Gaussian) broadening; sliders for S, ħω, solvent width and temperature show the mirror image, the Stokes shift and hot bands.

lessons.title: The Jablonski Diagram as Rate Physics
objectives: Write the first-order kinetic scheme for S₁ (radiative k_r, internal conversion k_ic, intersystem crossing k_isc) and derive the fluorescence quantum yield Φ = k_r/(k_r + k_nr) and lifetime τ = 1/(k_r + k_nr).
Link k_r to the Einstein A coefficient and oscillator strength (k_r ≈ 0.667 ν̃² f for n = 1) and use it to explain why strongly absorbing dyes have nanosecond lifetimes.
Derive the Stern–Volmer law τ₀/τ = 1 + k_qτ₀[Q] and explain Kasha's rule from the competition between ps vibrational relaxation and ns emission.

lectures.title: Lecture 34: Electronic Spectroscopy and Photochemistry

demoIdeas: Jablonski kinetics simulator: sliders for k_r, k_ic, k_isc and k_P; plot S₁ and T₁ populations versus time, emission decays and the quantum-yield bar chart, with a quencher slider showing Stern–Volmer behaviour.

lessons.title: Spin–Orbit Coupling, Intersystem Crossing and Phosphorescence
objectives: Explain why singlet–triplet transitions are spin-forbidden and how the spin–orbit operator mixes singlet character into the triplet with coefficient ⟨S|H_SO|T⟩/ΔE, so that the radiative rate is k_P ≈ |coefficient|²·k_S.
Apply the El-Sayed rule (ISC is faster between states of different orbital type, e.g. ¹(n,π*) → ³(π,π*)) and the heavy-atom effect (H_SO grows roughly as Z⁴).
Estimate a phosphorescence lifetime and say why it is microseconds to seconds, and why triplet states are long-lived enough to be quenched by O₂ (singlet-oxygen sensitization).

demoIdeas: Singlet/triplet energy diagram: pick orbital types (n,π* or π,π*) and an atomic number; sliders for the gap and H_SO show ISC rate, singlet admixture and the resulting phosphorescence lifetime.

units.title: Spin in a Field: Precession, Pulses, Bloch Equations and the FID
units.summary: The physics of a spin in a magnetic field: Zeeman Hamiltonian, Larmor precession (classical and quantum pictures agree), the rotating frame, RF pulses as rotations, Bloch equations with T₁ and T₂, and how the FID becomes the spectrum you read every day by Fourier transform.

lessons.title: Spin, the Magnetic Moment and the Zeeman Hamiltonian
objectives: State the spin-1/2 algebra ([I_x, I_y] = iI_z, eigenvalues ±½), the moment μ = γħI and the Zeeman Hamiltonian H = −γB₀I_z, giving a splitting ħ|γ|B₀ and a Larmor frequency ω₀ = −γB₀.
Compute Larmor frequencies of ¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁵N, ³¹P and ¹⁹F at a given field from γ, and explain what the sign of γ does to which spin state is lower in energy.

Give the thermal polarization P ≈ ħγB₀/2kT, show why it is tiny at room temperature, and explain the consequence: the bulk magnetization M₀ ∝ γ²B₀/T and the signal-to-noise ratio grows faster than linearly with field.

lectures.title: Lecture 1 (Chapter 3): Energy levels
Magnetic Resonance, Season 1, Episode 1A: Spin as a fundamental physical property
QMech8: Spin

demoIdeas: Zeeman level diagram versus B₀ with a nucleus selector (¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁵N, ³¹P, ¹⁹F, electron): shows ν₀, ΔE/kT and polarization, with a dot cloud of up/down spins whose imbalance is visible only after magnification.

lessons.title: Larmor Precession: Classical and Quantum Pictures Agree
objectives: Derive the classical torque equation dμ/dt = γμ × B and show that its solutions precess about B at ω = −γB.

Show from the Schrödinger/Heisenberg equations that ⟨I⟩ obeys exactly the same equation, and interpret precession as the phase e^{iω₀t} building up between α and β in the superposition cos(θ/2)|α⟩ + e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|β⟩.

Explain why the bulk magnetization of uncoupled spins can be treated as a classical vector, and why that picture fails for coupled spins (setting up the density-operator and product-operator treatment).

lectures.title: Lecture 2 (Chapter 4): The vector model

demoIdeas: Bloch sphere with a single spin: set polar angle and phase, choose a field direction, and watch the classical vector precess while the quantum expectation values ⟨I_x⟩, ⟨I_y⟩, ⟨I_z⟩ (from the state amplitudes) trace the same curve.

lessons.title: The Rotating Frame and RF Pulses as Rotations
objectives: Transform to a frame rotating at the transmitter frequency and show that H_rot = ΩI_z + ω₁(cosφ I_x + sinφ I_y) with offset Ω = ω₀ − ω_rf, giving an effective field of magnitude √(Ω² + ω₁²) tilted from z by tan θ = ω₁/Ω.
Show that an on-resonance pulse of length τ rotates the magnetization through β = ω₁τ about the pulse axis, and compute 90° and 180° durations and the B₁ amplitude from ω₁/2π.

Explain off-resonance effects (tilted effective field, excitation bandwidth of order ω₁/2π) and why hard pulses are needed to cover ¹³C shift ranges; relate the result to the Rabi oscillation of the optical two-level problem.

lectures.title: Lecture 2 (Chapter 4): The vector model
Magnetic Resonance, Season 1, Episode 4: Bloch equations and the rotating frame

demoIdeas: Bloch-sphere magnetization: choose pulse angle, phase and resonance offset, watch the vector nutate about the effective field in the rotating frame, then see the resulting FID and its Fourier transform change as the offset is swept.

lessons.title: The Bloch Equations: T₁, T₂ and Recovery
objectives: Write the Bloch equations with relaxation and solve them for free precession (an oscillating FID decaying as e^{−t/T₂}) and for recovery of M_z (saturation recovery and inversion recovery).

Distinguish T₁ (energy exchange with the lattice; populations) from T₂ (loss of phase coherence) and from T₂* (including field inhomogeneity), and state the physical reason T₂ ≤ 2T₁ (T₂ ≈ T₁ in small mobile molecules).
Choose a recycle delay: 5T₁ recovers 99.3% of M₀, the inversion-recovery null is at T₁ln2, and the Ernst angle cos θ_E = e^{−T_R/T₁} maximizes steady-state signal for repeated scans.

lessons.title: From FID to Spectrum: the Fourier Transform
objectives: Write the FID as a sum of damped complex exponentials Σ A_k e^{iω_kt − t/T₂k} and show that its complex Fourier transform has a real absorption (Lorentzian) part and an imaginary dispersion part, with FWHM 1/(πT₂).

Explain quadrature detection (two receiver phases) as the way to distinguish positive from negative frequencies, and the multiplex advantage of exciting all lines with one short pulse compared with a swept experiment (links to the E1 DSP elective).
Describe zero- and first-order phase correction and why a mis-phased line shows dispersive wings.

lessons.title: Sampling, Resolution and Apodisation in FT-NMR
objectives: Compute dwell time, acquisition time and digital resolution from the spectral width and number of points (Δt = 1/SW, T_acq = NΔt, δν = 1/T_acq) and explain how peaks outside the spectral window fold back.

Describe apodisation: exponential multiplication adds a Lorentzian line broadening LB, the matched filter maximizes S/N (LB ≈ natural width), and Gaussian or sine-bell windows trade S/N for resolution; zero filling interpolates but adds no information.
Predict the resulting linewidth (FWHM = natural + LB) and the truncation wiggles from a FID that has not decayed, and choose acquisition and processing parameters for a stated goal.

lessons.title: Spin Echoes, T₂ and Refocusing
objectives: Explain the Hahn echo 90°ₓ–τ–180°ᵧ–τ: a π pulse reverses the phase accumulated by each isochromat, so static field inhomogeneity and chemical-shift offsets are refocused at 2τ, and the echo amplitude decays with the true T₂ (not T₂*).
Show with the rotating-frame picture and with the density operator that the net phase is Ωτ − Ωτ = 0, and explain how CPMG trains measure T₂ and suppress dephasing from slow diffusion and exchange.
State what an echo does not refocus: a nonselective 180° does not refocus J-coupling evolution between homonuclear partners, which sets up the J-modulation of the product-operator lessons.

units.title: The Spin Hamiltonian: Shielding, J-Coupling and Strong Coupling
units.summary: The terms of the liquid-state NMR Hamiltonian that produce the shifts and multiplets you read: chemical shift as shielding, the scalar coupling Hamiltonian, multiplets from the energy levels, the AB strong-coupling problem solved exactly, and the anisotropic interactions that tumbling averages away.

lessons.title: The Chemical Shift as Shielding
objectives: Write the shielded Zeeman interaction ω = −γB₀(1 − σ) and explain why the ppm scale δ = (ν − ν_ref)/ν_ref × 10⁶ is independent of B₀ while shifts in Hz grow linearly with field.

Decompose σ into diamagnetic and paramagnetic parts, and explain ring-current and bond-anisotropy effects (benzene, alkynes, C=O) as induced local fields that depend on molecular orientation (σ is a tensor).
Convert between ppm and Hz, and use Δν/J to judge when first-order analysis is safe.

lessons.title: The J-Coupling Hamiltonian

Use the Karplus relation ³J(θ) = A cos²θ + B cosθ + C to connect J to dihedral angle, and contrast J with dipolar coupling (isotropic versus traceless).

Estimate a dipolar coupling in kHz for a given distance and connect it to why the same interaction, fluctuating, is the dominant source of relaxation.

units.title: Density Matrix, Product Operators and Multidimensional NMR
units.summary: The quantum machinery behind modern pulse sequences: the density operator, rotations of operators, product operators for coupled spins, J-modulated echoes, coherence selection, INEPT polarization transfer, and 2D NMR (COSY, HSQC) as a two-time Fourier transform.

lessons.title: The Density Operator: Populations and Coherences
objectives: Define the density operator ρ = Σ p_k|ψ_k⟩⟨ψ_k| for an ensemble, show ⟨A⟩ = Tr(ρA), and distinguish pure from mixed states; diagonal elements are populations and off-diagonal elements are coherences.
Write the thermal equilibrium state ρ_eq ≈ ½(1 + (ħγB₀/kT)I_z) in the high-temperature limit, and explain why the identity part can be dropped.
Map ρ onto observables: ⟨I_x⟩ and ⟨I_y⟩ come from the real and imaginary parts of the α–β coherence, so transverse magnetization is a coherence between Zeeman states.

lessons.title: Liouville–von Neumann Evolution: Pulses and Shifts as Rotations
objectives: Derive dρ/dt = −i[H, ρ] from the Schrödinger equation and its solution ρ(t) = e^{−iHt}ρ(0)e^{iHt}.

Prove with the commutator series that e^{−iφI_z} I_x e^{iφI_z} = I_x cos φ + I_y sin φ (and cyclic permutations), so chemical-shift precession and RF pulses rotate the operators in Cartesian space exactly like the Bloch vector.
Compute an observable by this route: equilibrium I_z, a 90°ₓ pulse and free evolution at offset Ω gives the signal Tr(ρ I_+) ∝ e^{iΩt}.
keyEquations: e^{-i\phi\hat I_z}\hat I_xe^{i\phi\hat I_z}=\hat I_x\cos\phi+\hat I_y\sin\phi

lessons.title: Product Operators for Two Coupled Spins
objectives: Build the 16-element Cartesian basis for two spins-½ (½E, I_k, S_k, 2I_kS_l), distinguish in-phase from anti-phase terms, and say which are observable and how they look (in-phase doublet versus anti-phase doublet).
Apply the three evolution rules: chemical shift (rotation about z), J-coupling (I_x → I_x cos πJt + 2I_yS_z sin πJt) and pulses (rotations), to follow a simple sequence term by term.
Interpret a product operator physically: 2I_xS_z is the I coherence with a sign set by the S state, i.e. the difference between the two lines of the I doublet.

lessons.title: Spin Echoes with Coupling: J-Modulation and Editing
objectives: Analyse the spin echo τ–180°–τ for a coupled I–S pair: a 180° on both spins refocuses the shift but lets J evolve (cos 2πJτ modulation), a 180° on one spin refocuses J but not the shift of the other, using product-operator rules.
Derive the multiplicity-dependent factor cos^n(πJT) of the attached-proton test (APT) and use it to assign CH₃, CH₂, CH and C.
Explain why this J-modulation is the basis of INEPT, HSQC and DEPT, and why the homonuclear echo carries the modulation of all couplings.

lessons.title: Coherence Order, Phase Cycling and Gradient Selection
objectives: Define coherence order p (the change in total magnetic quantum number), identify observable single-quantum (p = ±1), zero- and double-quantum terms, and show that a z-rotation by φ multiplies coherence p by e^{−ipφ}.
Explain how phase cycling exploits this phase dependence to select a coherence transfer pathway, and how pulsed field gradients do it in a single scan by dephasing coherence in proportion to pγGτ.
Work out the gradient ratio needed to select a stated pathway, e.g. G₁/G₂ = γ_H/γ_C ≈ 4 for a ¹³C → ¹H transfer in HSQC.

lessons.title: INEPT: Polarization Transfer from a High-γ Spin
objectives: Follow INEPT with product operators (90°ₓ(H) – τ – 180°(H,C) – τ – 90°(H,C), τ = 1/4J): ¹H polarization becomes anti-phase ¹³C coherence, with enhancement γ_H/γ_C ≈ 4 for ¹³C and ≈ 10 for ¹⁵N.
Distinguish polarization transfer (a coherent process under J) from the NOE (cross-relaxation), and explain why the repetition rate depends on the ¹H T₁ rather than the slow ¹³C T₁.
Choose the refocusing delay to edit CH, CH₂ and CH₃ multiplicities using n·sin(2πJΔ)cos^{n−1}(2πJΔ), and state what decoupling requires.

lessons.title: Two-Dimensional NMR as a Two-Time Fourier Transform

Explain how F₁ frequency discrimination (States, States-TPPI, echo-antiecho) preserves phase-sensitive absorptive line shapes, and what 'phase twist' and magnitude mode cost in resolution.
Compute the resolution and duration of a 2D experiment from the number of increments, the spectral width in F₁ and the scans per increment.

Read a COSY or HSQC spectrum as a map of coherence pathways, and say why small J couplings give weak cross peaks (anti-phase components cancel when lines are broader than J).

units.title: Relaxation Theory: Spectral Densities, BPP, NOE and Exchange
units.summary: Relaxation as statistical mechanics of fluctuating local fields: correlation functions and spectral densities, BPP rates and the T₁ minimum, Redfield theory and detailed balance, the Solomon equations and the NOE, distance measurement, and exchange.

lessons.title: Relaxation from Fluctuating Fields: Correlation Functions and Spectral Densities
objectives: Model relaxation as a spin Hamiltonian H₀ + H₁(t) with a random local field, define the correlation function G(τ) = ⟨b(t)b(t+τ)⟩ = ⟨b²⟩e^{−|τ|/τ_c} and its Fourier transform, the spectral density J(ω) = 2τ_c/(1 + ω²τ_c²) (per unit ⟨b²⟩).
Explain by the golden rule that transitions between Zeeman levels are driven by the power of the fluctuation at the transition frequency, J(ω₀), so T₁ probes motion at ω₀ while T₂ also feels J(0).
Estimate a rotational correlation time from the Stokes–Einstein–Debye relation τ_c = 4πηa³/3kT and describe how it scales with size, viscosity and temperature.

lessons.title: BPP Theory: T₁, T₂ and the Correlation Time
objectives: Write the dipolar (BPP) rates for like spins-½, R₁ = (3/10)b²[τ_c/(1+ω₀²τ_c²) + 4τ_c/(1+4ω₀²τ_c²)] and the corresponding R₂, and show that in extreme narrowing both reduce to (3/2)b²τ_c.
Locate the T₁ minimum near ω₀τ_c ≈ 0.6 and explain why T₂ keeps shrinking as τ_c grows while T₁ passes through a minimum and then lengthens with field.
Apply to real molecules: why small molecules give sharp lines with T₁ ≈ T₂ of seconds, why proteins have T₂ ≪ T₁ and broad lines, and what cooling or viscosity does.

lessons.title: Redfield Theory and Why Relaxation Reaches Boltzmann Equilibrium
objectives: Outline Redfield theory: second-order perturbation theory in H₁(t) with the Born–Markov and secular approximations gives dσ/dt = −i[H₀, σ] − Γ̂(σ − σ_eq), with rates built from spectral densities at the transition frequencies.

Explain why a classical symmetric J(ω) would drive the spins to infinite temperature, and how detailed balance, W↑/W↓ = e^{−ħω₀/kT} (the quantum fluctuation–dissipation relation), makes the steady state the thermal state of the lattice.
Quantify the size of the correction at NMR frequencies (~10⁻⁵) versus EPR (~10⁻³) and say why the 'classical' BPP formulas are still accurate yet T₁ returns M_z to M₀ and not to zero.

objectives: Write the Solomon equations for two dipole-coupled spins with transition probabilities W₀, W₁, W₂, identify auto-relaxation ρ and cross-relaxation σ = W₂ − W₀, and derive the steady-state enhancement η = (σ/ρ)(γ_S/γ_I).

objectives: Describe the NOESY build-up a_ij(τ_m) ≈ σ_ijτ_m at short mixing time, σ ∝ r⁻⁶, and calibrate an unknown distance from a reference pair, r = r_ref(a_ref/a)^{1/6}.

units.title: MRI, EPR and Synthesis

lessons.title: MRI: Gradients as Position Encoding and k-Space

Explain slice selection (band-limited RF pulse with a gradient: thickness = bandwidth/(γG/2π)), frequency and phase encoding, and how field of view = 1/Δk and resolution = 1/(2k_max) follow from sampling theory.
Compute gradient-induced frequency spreads and slice thicknesses, and relate T₁/T₂ contrast to the Bloch equations through repetition and echo times.
